en: Whatever is spoken by me through the grace of the glorious Gāyatrī, let that be accepted as a virtue by those who can discern between merit and fault. (1)
In the Sāṃkhya philosophy, the union of the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is declared to be the primary cause of the world as it is perceived. (2)

In the Sāṃkhya philosophy, this conjunction of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is declared to be the primary cause of the world as it is perceived. "The conjunction of both is like that of a lame man and a blind man; from that, creation proceeds"—this statement from the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* is the authority here. Nature (*prakṛti*) shall have the designation "field," while the person (*puruṣa*) is called the "knower of the field."
Through its conjunction with that [Puruṣa], this world is always illuminated by nature.
That state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) is indeed called Prakṛti; for these three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are so designated by virtue of their effects. (4)

Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities (guṇas). Their state of equilibrium alone is called Prakṛti. Vācaspatimiśra states: "The state of equilibrium among sattva, rajas, and tamas is Prakṛti. The first creation from that is the intellect (buddhi); the second would be the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti). From the ego-sense arises the subtle element (tanmātra), which is the cause of the gross elements. (Verse 5)

The first creation from Prakṛti is called Mahat, which is the intellect (buddhi). The second creation is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). From this very ahaṅkāra, the subtle elements (tanmātras), which are the causes of the gross elements, have arisen.
Likewise, the eleven organs—the ten senses and the one [mind]—are the modifications of ahaṅkāra.
That which is the predominant quality within that ahaṅkāra, he is devoted to that. (6)
In the Vaikṛta [ego], Sattva is predominant; in the Taijasa, Rajas is said to be so;
and in the Tāmasa, Tamas is primary. Indeed, these designations are to be understood according to their effects.

The eleven sense organs are indeed modifications of the *ahaṅkāra* (ego). For instance, whichever quality (*guṇa*) is predominant in the *ahaṅkāra*, that *ahaṅkāra* becomes oriented toward that very quality. In the *vaikṛta-ahaṅkāra*, the *sattva* quality is predominant; in the *taijasa-ahaṅkāra*, the *rajas* quality; and in the *tāmasa-ahaṅkāra*, the *tamas* quality. Thus, the designation [of these types] should be understood solely from their effects. There are exactly five organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) and five organs of action (*karmendriya*).
The effect of the *ahaṅkāra* consists of the mind (*manas*), which is the internal organ (*antarindriya*). (8)

The eye, the ear, the tongue, the nose, and the skin—these are the five organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*). Likewise, speech, the hands, the feet, the anus, and the generative organ—these are the five organs of action (*karmendriya*). And the mind (*manas*) is the internal organ. Thus, the eleven organs arise from the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*) assisted by the *taijasa* ego. The twenty-fifth Sāṃkhya Karika, along with Gauḍapāda’s commentary, should be consulted.

"The ego, the Great One (*mahat*), the intellect (*citta*), and the mind—these four are regarded as the internal instrument (*antaḥ-karaṇa*) in the systems of philosophy; they receive a single name based on their function. (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 9)

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is indeed one; however, due to differences in its functions (*vṛttibheda*), it is described in the [Sāṃkhya] system as *ahaṅkāra*, *mahat*, *citta*, and *manas*. But in the Yoga system, due to differences in function, only a threefold nature—consisting of *mahat*, *ahaṅkāra*, and *manas*—is well-established, not a fourfold one. As for the inclusion of *citta* within *mahat* (which is synonymous with *buddhi*) in this view, one should look solely at the words of Vijñānabhikṣu:
"A threefold division is seen in the effect, and likewise unity in the instrument;
every effect is produced in reality from the cause alone. (10)
For since the primary cause (pradhāna) is the object of action, the threefold nature (triguṇya) is attributed to the mind;
therefore, the activity of the qualities (guṇas) is observed in the mind under the name of "function" (vṛtti). || 11 ||

The mind, which is produced from the *pradhāna* consisting of the three *guṇas*, is itself also composed of the three *guṇas*. This is according to the principle that "the qualities of the cause initiate the qualities of the effect. For this very reason, activity known as *vṛtti* (modification) is observed among the *guṇas* within the mind.
"That by which this consciousness (*citta*) is supported is known as *sattva*; that by which it is known is *rajas*; and that which is to be known is *tamas*.
All these are mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*), just like the various modes of conduct of a Brahmin. (12)

"The functions of the mind are said to be those activities, such as the operations of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, by which the mind lives, just as the performance of sacrifices and other rites are for the twice-born. This statement by Vijñānabhikṣu is the authority here; it should be understood that the very existence of the mind consists in its function alone. For this reason, when the functions are restrained, the mind itself is also restrained.
Indeed, the functions of the mind are proclaimed to be innumerable;
yet, when enumerated in one place, there are five functions known as powers (*śakti*). (13)
The first modification is valid cognition; the second is error;
the third is called conceptualization; sleep is another; and memory is the fifth. (14)
In the treatise, the wise declare that experience corresponding to reality is valid cognition (pramā);
and the instrument (karaṇa) of that valid cognition is proclaimed in the treatise as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 15 ||
Perception, inference, and verbal testimony—these three are the means of valid cognition for the determination of reality; by them alone is everything established. (16)
Valid cognition arising from the conjunction of the sense faculty and its object is perception; that is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which serves as the cause for inference. ||17||

Following the principle that "the establishment of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is indeed from the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*"), three means of knowledge are accepted in the Yoga system: perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and verbal testimony (*śabda*). Through these three means of knowledge, everything is established for the determination of reality in the Yoga system. When the sense organ is in contact with its object, the cognition that arises—and its instrument as well—is perception. Inference also proceeds by being based upon perception itself; for through a present connection, one infers what has already occurred and what is yet to occur.
For the knowledge that arises therein is indeed inference as a means of valid cognition. 18.
When the knowledge of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) arises from the mark (liṅga) which possesses pervasion (vyāpti),
that valid cognition is inference (anumiti), and here the inferential process (anumāna) is the cause.

When the knowledge of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) arises from a mark (*liṅga*) characterized by invariable concomitance (*niyata-sāhacarya*), there is "inference" (*anumiti*) as the valid cognition (*pramā*) and "inference" (*anumāna*) as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The words of one who perceives reality and is free from doubt, as well as the Vedas and the elders, are to be understood as valid means of knowledge for the determination of truth. (19)
That cognition which is not established in that [true] form and is devoid of truthfulness is called ignorance (avidyā); in Yoga, its designation is "error" (viparyaya). || 20 ||
Knowledge that is unestablished in its true nature as consciousness and permeated by falsity is called "error" (*viparyaya*) in Yoga; it is a synonym for *avidyā*.

That mental modification (*vṛtti*) which, being devoid of a real object, follows upon verbal knowledge is renowned as "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*); this is to be understood according to the *Yogadarśana*. (21)
When the waking state and the dream state are both overwhelmed by tamas, that state is called sleep (nidrā).
At that time, there arises a state of darkness characterized by the absence of other mental modifications; this turbid functioning of the mind's essence is known as sleep. (23)
That sleep has the nature of a mental modification (vṛtti) is understood from memory alone;
for the memory experienced during the waking state is exactly like that of sleep. (24)
Without a mental modification (vṛtti), how can there be knowledge? In the absence of knowledge, how can there be memory?
Therefore, sleep must be a mental modification, for memory exists during the waking state.

When the waking and dreaming functions are overwhelmed by the deluding darkness (tamas), and other functions have ceased due to that state of darkness, then the impure function of the mind in the form of a positive mental modification is called "sleep. It should be understood that the memory which arises immediately after sleep in the waking state is of the same nature as sleep itself. Memory is dependent upon experience, and experience is dependent upon mental modifications; therefore, sleep is a mental modification (cittavṛtti). A modification of the mind that grasps what has already been grasped is called memory.
It cannot be less than the original experience, nor can it ever be more. (26)

That mental modification which grasps only an object already grasped is called "memory" (*smṛti*). The meaning is that it is a modification whose object is not greater than the object present in the original experience. Whatever extent of an object we experience, we remember that much or less, but never more than that.
If the definition were stated simply as "that which grasps what has been grasped," there would be a fault;
for in that case, over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would result, as it would apply to knowledge (*jñāna*) that possesses a recurring form (*anugatākāra*). (Verse 27)
There is no over-extension in that definition because of their distinct forms;
nor is the object deficient in a cognition that possesses a recurring form. (28)

Even in a cognition whose object is a single thing, such as "pot, pot, pot," there is the quality of apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*); thus, there would be the contingency of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). However, in this [perceptual] cognition, the object is not less than the previously apprehended object. In memory (*smṛti*), on the other hand, the object is "not more than the object of the original experience" (*anubhavaviṣayādanadhikaviṣaya*); therefore, there is no lack of extension (*avyāpti*) there. The *Yogasiddhāntacandrikā* should be consulted here.
Yoga is defined as the restraint (*nirodha*) of the mind along with its fluctuations (*vṛtti*). This yoga, which is synonymous with meditation (*samādhi*), is called *Rājayoga*. || 30 ||

Yoga, concentration (*samādhi*), and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) are synonymous. This concentration, which has an object of meditation (*dhyeya*), is twofold: the first is cognitive concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*), and the second is non-cognitive (*asamprajñāta*).
When the object of meditation is clearly perceived within concentration through the restraint of the mind, then that concentration is to be known as cognitive; it is of four kinds. (31)
With vitarka and vicāra, with ānanda and asmitā—thus the four divisions of samprajñāta-samādhi are proclaimed in Yoga. (32)

That concentration in which the object of meditation is correctly discerned is called "cognitive" (samprajñāta). Its four divisions are: concentration with deliberation (savitarka), concentration with reflection (savicāra), concentration with bliss (sānanda), and concentration with the sense of "I-am-ness" (sāsmitā). In deliberation, the support for the mind is the gross physical realm composed of the five elements;
likewise, in reflection, it is the subtle cause of the elements, consisting of the tanmātras. (33)

When the mind, having taken as its object the gross [elements] composed of the five elements, remains focused on that gross object, then that concentration is called "with vitarka" (savitarka). And when it takes as its object the subtle [objects], such as the *tanmātras* and so forth, then it is called "with vicāra" (savicāra).
This objective field is the first stage in yoga for the restraint of the mind;
the stages "with bliss" (sānanda) and "with self-sense" (sāsmita) follow later, preceded by the act of grasping.
When there is a state of oneness between the intellect and the Puruṣa, the grasper, that is the samādhi called "I-am-ness" (asmitā); at that time, the Puruṣa itself becomes the object. || 35 ||
However, when there is direct realization due to the excellence of the sentient being's capacity, then bliss becomes manifest as that which is to be known, for it truly gladdens him. (36)

When the intellect (*buddhi*) attains oneness with the Puruṣa, the grasper, that is the concentration (*samādhi*) called "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*). Regarding this, the Commentary states: "The cognition consisting of a single essence is *asmitā*. The meaning is that it is called *asmitā* because its form consists of nothing more than the thought "I am. The direct experience of the joy arising from the excellence of the *sattva* quality is "bliss" (*ānanda*). Commentators explain that this bliss is a property of the mind (*citta*). "When all those fluctuations have ceased in every respect, and only the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) remains in the yoga of the mind that has no other resort," (37)
For he who possesses supreme detachment as the cause of concentration,
that concentration known as "asamprajñāta" then shines forth.
Since this [state] is devoid of any object of meditation and rests upon the emptiness of entities, therefore detachment from the object of meditation is considered the cause for this samādhi. (39)

When all modifications [of the mind] have ceased and only residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) remain, that is "seedless" (*asamprajñāta*) samādhi. Detachment (*vairāgya*) is of two kinds: lower detachment and higher detachment. Among these, the first is the absence of craving for perceived objects such as women, food, and drink, as well as for [objects of the future] such as heaven. The latter is the opposition to craving regarding all activities of the *guṇas*; thereafter, when there is an equality of purity between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there is isolation (*kaivalya*).
Thus it has been said by the masters of yoga: "Through yoga, yoga is to be known."
In the same way, another yoga should be understood as being practiced gradually through the first [stage]. || 40 ||
The meaning is that through the practice of *samprajñāta-yoga*, one should gradually come to know *asamprajñāta-yoga*.
Yoga, which is to be accomplished by means of faith and other causal factors, is to be grasped by those seeking liberation, especially by practitioners of *rājayoga*. (41)

Faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—these are the causal factors beginning with faith. Because each preceding one generates the one immediately following it, they constitute the cause for absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Indeed, asamprajñāta samādhi is not easily attained merely through birth;
therefore, among gods and humans, it is certainly devoid [of those who possess] faith and the other qualities. 42.
For those who are bodiless (videha), whose bodies consist of the sixfold sheaths (ṣaṭkauśika), and who are dissolving into primordial nature (prakṛti), that very state is called samādhi. (43)
Therefore, ignorance alone should be known as the false nature of existence, since ignorance is its root; thus, it must indeed be abandoned for the sake of yoga.

Non-discerning [samādhi] is of two kinds: that caused by means (upāyapratyaya) and that caused by existence (bhavapratyaya). For those seeking liberation, the first-mentioned is the one caused by means; the second, caused by existence, has ignorance as its cause and belongs to the bodiless (videha) and those merged in primordial matter (prakṛtilaya). The bodiless are those devoid of the body composed of the six sheaths—flesh, blood, hair, fat, bone, and marrow—and having dissolved into the elements and the senses immediately after the fall of the physical body.

Those who have realized any one of the unmanifest (avyakta), the great principle (mahat), the ego (ahaṅkāra), or the five subtle elements (tanmātra) as the Self, and who, through the worship of those [principles], become dissolved in the causes such as primordial nature (prakṛti) after the fall of the body, are known as "dissolved in nature" (prakṛtilaya). Since ignorance is the root of the non-cognitive samādhi (asamprajñāta-samādhi) which has worldly existence (bhava) as its condition, that [ignorance] must be abandoned.
This samādhi is easily accomplished through the cause of intense momentum;
there are various means that bestow the perfection of samādhi. (45)

For those with intense dispassion (*tīvra-vairāgya*), *samādhi* is easily accomplished. For those who possess swiftness in the practice of these means, the attainment of *samādhi* is near at hand. Vācaspatimiśra stated, "Yoga has faith as its root," and the Lord [Kṛṣṇa] said, "Whatever one's faith is, that indeed he is"; both of these establish the primacy of faith (*śraddhā*). Bhaktiyoga, Kriyāyoga, and likewise Caryāyoga;
Karmayoga, Haṭha, Mantra, Jñānayoga, and Layayoga. (46)
Non-duality, the goal, yoga, perfection, Brahman, and likewise Śiva, as well as latent impressions and the yoga of meditation—all these are shown in the aphorisms. || 47 ||

The author of the *Yogasiddhāntacandrikā*, Nārāyaṇatīrtha Svāmin, has pointed out that the fifteen types of yoga can be understood from the *Pātañjalayogasūtras* themselves; the details therein should be consulted. When Īśvara is pleased through devotion, He bestows liberation quickly;
therefore, obstacles do not arise from the practice of devotion to Īśvara. (48)
The Puruṣa, never touched by afflictions, karma, and their results, nor by the conditioned factors that possess form, is considered the Lord (Īśvara). 49.
He is omniscient, omnipresent, and transcends all time;
because He is also the cause of time itself, the Lord is said to be eternal.
By constantly reciting the *prāṇava* and likewise by contemplating its meaning, the mind becomes one-pointed and the Supreme Self is revealed. (51)
Therefore, no obstacles arise from this meditation on the Lord, and the knowledge of his own true nature also arises for this yogi. (52)
The obstacles, which cause hindrances, should be understood as distractions;
distraction arises when the mind falls away from that meditation. (53)

"Sickness, languor, doubt, carelessness, laziness, lack of dispassion, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage [of concentration], and instability—these are the distractions of the mind; they are the obstacles," so says the *Yoga Sūtra*.
Furthermore, the *Yoga Sūtra* should be consulted here: "Pain, mental distress, trembling of the body, and labored breathing and exhaling are co-existent with these distractions.
Just as Īśvara is pure, serene, and the absolute Person (puruṣa),...
Likewise, the individual soul (jīva) is the perceiver of the intellect and is devoid of birth and other such attributes. || 54 ||
In this way, the intellect of the yogi established in samādhi arises, indeed filled with the knowledge of the true nature of the individual self and the supreme self. 55.
When the mind is afflicted by those distractions, then that self-controlled practitioner should strive to refine it through practice. 56.

The wise person should cultivate a sense of friendship toward others upon their attainment of happiness; likewise, one should cultivate compassion for the suffering of the wicked and joy toward their merit. (57)
And likewise, the wise person should constantly cultivate equanimity toward non-meritorious actions;
thus one attains a serene mind—this is called the yoga of conduct. (58)
The vital breath (prāṇa) is primarily the wind; for a human being is indeed supported by the vital breath.
Through the regulation of the breath (prāṇāyāma), the restraint of the mind is always easily attained.
With effort, one should properly expel the air from the abdomen through the passage of the nostrils slowly; this is called praśvāsa (exhalation). || 60 ||
The retention of the exhaled breath outside [the body] is considered *kumbhaka*; the inhalation (*śvāsa*), exhalation (*praśvāsa*), and retention (*kumbha*) together are called *haṭhayoga*. (61)

The scriptural statements, such as "Haṭhayoga is proclaimed to be Prāṇāyāma" and "The unification of the sun and the moon is designated as Haṭha," serve as the authority establishing that Prāṇāyāma is indeed Haṭhayoga. Furthermore, if a yogi directs his mental activity toward objects such as fragrance and the like, his mind will certainly become devoid of doubt.
The cognitions of sound and the other sense objects, when practiced with the mind, eliminate doubt;
thereby, through that yoga of practice, pure faith increases.

Through the practice of concentration (*lakṣya-yoga*) by restraining the mind at the tip of the nose and other such points, there arises direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of those respective objects; from that, faith (*śraddhā*) arises, and by means of that, the mind becomes steady in meditation and the like. Thus, through the aforementioned direct perception, doubts in the mind are removed.

Furthermore, that activity known as mere self-consciousness (*asmitā-mātra*), which consists of the awareness of the intellect (*buddhi-saṃveda-rūpiṇī*), is capable of obstructing the stability of the mind. (64)
In this verse of the sūtra, "The yoga of Brahman is free from sorrow," the Yoga of Śiva is also indicated by way of the context of its luminosity.

In this Yoga Sūtra, "The [meditative state] free from sorrow or luminous," a certain mental activity that binds the mind to its steadiness is described. The *Yogasiddhāntacandrikā* states that this activity, which is devoid of the exhaustion caused by afflictions and has light as its object, indicates the yoga of Brahman and Śiva.

Alternatively: "When the mind is restrained, the mental consciousness of one who is dispassionate takes that [restrained] mind as its support; then, by that [support], the mind itself is restrained. (66)
The mind of one who possesses dispassion also attains stability through yoga. When the mind is taken up as being free from latent impressions (vāsanā), this yoga is called Vāsanā-yoga.
Whether in the form of a dream, or in the state of waking, or likewise in the knowledge of sleep, when the mind takes hold [of these], it attains stability. (67)

In a dream, the mind—predominated by *sattva* due to the influence of prior latent impressions (*pūrvavāsanā*)—perceives the form of the Blessed One; likewise, at the onset of sleep, one should attain stability by making that very bliss which is experienced the object of focus for the mind. The *Candrikā* states that this too is a sub-division of the yoga of latent impressions (*vāsanā-yoga*). Whatever object the mind, corrupted by the imbalance of the *guṇas*, takes as its support, one should meditate upon that alone with undivided attention; by that means, the mind is restrained. (68)
This method of yoga is called *dhyānayoga* (the yoga of meditation). It is defined in the *Yogasiddhāntacandrikā* as "meditation upon objects as desired, in accordance with one's inclination.
The knower of yoga attains mastery over both the gross and the subtle;
[that mastery is supreme in the gross, and in the subtle, it extends even to the atom]. (69)

For the mind of a yogin, as it enters into the subtle, attains a state of stability down to the level of the atom, and likewise in the gross and the immensely large. This is the yoga of accomplishment (siddhiyoga). Just as a crystal assumes a form through proximity to an adjunct (upādhi), so too does the mind assume a form when colored by the object of perception (grāhya). || 70 ||

Just as a pure crystal assumes the form of red or other colors due to the proximity of limiting adjuncts such as the hibiscus flower, so too does the mind assume the form of the object of perception and so forth. The sequential abiding of the mind within the Puruṣa, the senses, and the elements, resulting in the attainment of their respective forms, is called *samāpatti* (meditative absorption). || 71 ||

That meditative attainment (samāpatti) which is thoroughly intermingled with conceptual constructions (vikalpa) regarding words, meanings, and cognitions—each having distinct forms—is called "with reasoning" (savitarka). || 72 ||

The properties of sound, such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth, reside in the word; qualities such as insentience (*jāḍya*) and so forth reside in the object; and others, such as luminosity and formlessness, reside in cognition. (73)
Even though diversity prevails, everything in every respect maintains its oneness; likewise, all things—consisting of word, meaning, and cognition—participate in that same unity. (74)

When the word "cow" is uttered, the word, the object, and the cognition appear in the world as mutually non-different—[as if thinking] "the word is 'cow'," "the object is 'cow'," and "the cognition is 'cow'"—because they are perceived as distinct only through their attributes (*dharma*). This other [type of] perception arises from a connection with a trace of ignorance (*avidyā-leśa*).
That meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) which appears as the mere thing-in-itself when memory has been purified is called "the objectless" (*nirvicāra*). (75)
Emptiness shines forth within that [cognition], yet there is no emptiness of its own nature;
likewise, the object appears intensely within it in a non-conceptual manner. (76)
In the same way, there is a corresponding meditative absorption (samāpatti) regarding the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma);
it is renowned as "with deliberation" (savicārā), for its object is indeed subtle.
That meditative attainment which is empty of dharmas such as tranquility, and likewise has a subtle object, is considered the non-discursive (nirvicārā) attainment, the fourth and supreme state. (78)

When the memory of conventions has been abandoned, that state in which there is the manifestation of an object free from conceptual construction is the *nirvitarka* (non-discursive) meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). The meditative attainment regarding subtle objects such as the *tanmātras* and *ahaṅkāra*, when they are still conceptually constructed, is *savicāra* (discursive). The meditative attainment regarding those very same objects, when they are devoid of specific qualities and consist of the mere object, is *nirvicāra* (non-discursive). In the *Siddhāntacandrikā*, this is seen to have another name: *samprajñāta-layayoga*. Furthermore, its status as having subtle objects is declared to extend up to *pradhāna*;
however, among all principles (*tattvas*), nothing exists beyond the *aliṅga* (the unmanifest). (79)
This samādhi would be "with seed" (sabīja) by virtue of the stages beginning with "with reasoning" (savitarka);
for ignorance is the seed, and that which is joined with it is "cognitive" (samprajñāta).
When the sattva of the intellect shines forth, free from impurities such as lack of purity and the like, then that is said to be the "nirvicāra" (objectless) samādhi. || 81 ||
Then there arises internal clarity, and the light of wisdom becomes manifest;
that is the wisdom which bears truth, for it constantly upholds reality. (82)
Since wisdom has excellence as its purpose and since it sustains that which is subtle,
it therefore attains a manifold variety through the cognitions derived from scripture and inference.
Other mental formations are ceased by the water of the formation of wisdom;
when those formations are ceased, there arises the seedless yoga that grants the desired goal. 84.
Since it is empty of the seeds of suffering, it is therefore called "without object";
for that concentration alone is the cause of liberation, in which the person indeed remains solitary.

The asamprajñāta-samādhi, which possesses the distinctions of being with *vitarka* and so forth, is called "seeded samādhi" (*sabīja-samādhi*) because of the existence of the seed in the form of ignorance (*avidyā*). However, when that [ignorance] is absent, it is "seedless samādhi" (*nirbīja-samādhi*). When one becomes proficient in the state of *nirvicāra* within seeded samādhi, then there is an intensification of *sattva*; when that occurs, the "truth-bearing" (*ṛtambharā*) wisdom arises. By the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the wisdom of samādhi, the impressions of the emergent state (*vyutthāna*) are suppressed. When even those impressions are ceased, there is seedless samādhi, and from that, liberation—this is the sequence to be understood.
Preceded by the recitation of purifying mantras beginning with the Praṇava,
one should perform austerity according to whatever capacity one possesses.
The dedication of all ritual acts, including their fruits, unto the Supreme Person who is the highest of all, is declared to be Kriyā-yoga. (84)
Concentration, which consists of cultivation, destroys the power of the afflictions;
it is accomplished through the yoga of action and bestows the fire of higher discernment.
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the clinging to life—these five are said in Yoga to be the afflictions that create obstacles. (86)
All afflictions depend upon ignorance, just as sprouts depend upon a seed;
they arise through ignorance alone, and they are extinguished by ignorance alone.

This [cognition] is of the nature of reality and not a non-entity; it consists of the form of a false cognition, by which a cognition of existence arises even with respect to an utterly non-existent object. (88)

Through the practice of yoga consisting of austerity (tapas), study (svādhyāya), and devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna), the attainment of samādhi and the destruction of the afflictions (kleśas) such as ignorance (avidyā) and the rest become possible. Just as a sprout grows depending upon a seed, so too do the four afflictions grow depending upon ignorance, and by that same [practice] they are destroyed. Furthermore, ignorance is not merely the absence of knowledge; because it possesses the capacity to produce distinct effects, it is indeed a form of knowledge itself. Between the Puruṣa and the intellect (buddhi), which are utterly distinct from one another, there arises a single-minded identification; this state of the intellect is designated as "I-am-ness" (asmitā). || 89 ||
The notion of non-difference between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the self (*puruṣa*), which are in fact absolutely distinct, is called *asmitā* (egoism).
Attachment to pleasure and its means is designated as *rāga* (passion).
Aversion toward pain and its means is designated as *dveṣa* (hatred). (90)

"The commentary states: 'Greed is a thirsting for pleasure or its means; that is attachment (*rāga*). Furthermore, the statement of Miśra should also be considered in this context: 'For even when an object of pleasure is being perceived, one desires it by recollecting that things of its kind have been causes of pleasure, or by inferring that this [object] is a cause of pleasure because it belongs to that same class.
"Indeed, even for the wise man, there is constant attachment while living.
The reason for this is that the affliction known as *abhiniveśa* (clinging to life) exists therein. (91)

This affliction flows by its own inherent nature; it is habituated to flowing in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*), and is not adventitious. The affliction known as "clinging" (*abhiniveśa*), which takes the form of the fear of death and is caused by the experience of the suffering of death in a previous birth—expressed as "May I not cease to exist; may I always live"—exists even in the wise man.
These afflictions, born of the mind, are to be abandoned through the dissolution of the mind.
The gross fluctuations of the afflictions are to be abandoned by the yogi through meditation. (92)
For while affliction exists, one indeed abides in both merit and demerit during life;
these are to be experienced just as in the present birth, so too in the unseen future birth.
Pleasure and pain arise for those two; their maturation (vipāka) is threefold.
This maturation, rooted in affliction (kleśa), consists of birth and so forth throughout one's life. (94)
Birth, lifespan, and wealth are considered the threefold maturation;
since these pertain to a single body, they are regarded as belonging to a single existence. (95)

From the five afflictions beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) consisting of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) become objects of experience in the present and future times. It is from merit and demerit alone that the fruits of pleasure and pain, as well as the maturation (*vipāka*) of birth and so forth, arise. Birth, the period of life, and experience—this triad is called "maturation" (*vipāka*). That there is the manifestation of the fruit within a single body is what is termed "pertaining to a single existence" (*ekabhavika*), as explained in the *Candrikā*.
The increase in the craving for the enjoyment of sense-objects that is observed among men is indeed called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*); it should be known as that which brings about suffering. (96)
But this "torment" (tāpa) is indeed hatred toward that which obstructs enjoyment;
it would be a latent impression (saṃskāra) causing the memory of enjoyment and yielding suffering. (97)
Or rather, for these three reasons, due to the imbalance of the qualities (guṇas), everything is suffering for the discerning person who experiences all objects of the senses. (98)
Through its experience, past suffering has been successfully passed over;
as for present suffering, it is yet to be experienced and is therefore not fit to be abandoned [at this moment]. (99)
Since future suffering afflicts the practitioner intensely, it must therefore be abandoned by the practitioner who desires reality. (100)
Likewise, the conjunction of the Puruṣa and the intellect is the cause of that which is to be abandoned;
though itself inactive, it is the visible cause of both experience and liberation. 101.

Sattva, rajas, and tamas—bestowing knowledge, activity, and delusion respectively—are the perceptible world consisting of the elements and the senses; they are the cause of both enjoyment and liberation. 102.
It has the form of objects such as sound and consists of the ascertainment of their nature.
Experience is the modification of the intellect; by means of that, the Puruṣa becomes as if bound.
The view is that liberation is simply the knower’s realization of its own true nature;
enjoyment and liberation do not belong to the person, but belong solely to the guṇas. (104)

Although this seer is pure consciousness alone, it appears as if subject to transformation due to its identification with the fluctuations of the intellect; yet, it rests upon the pure cognition. || 105 ||
That which consists of cause and effect is never for its own sake; rather, just as one desires [benefit] from others, the visible world exists for the sake of another.

It is lost for one who has achieved his purpose, yet it is not lost for one whose vision is deluded. There is no elision of the root *naś* (to perish); "destruction" (*nāśa*) means non-perception. || 107 ||
In the Yoga philosophy, the perception of this object of sight is considered to be what is called "experience" (bhoga), while the perception of the seer's own true nature is liberation (mokṣa). 108.
In the conjunction of the body and the mind, ignorance is considered the cause;
when that ignorance is destroyed, the conjunction likewise ceases. (109)
For this absence of conjunction is called "abandonment" by the wise;
in the state of isolation (kaivalya), the individual soul is isolated, or likewise, the qualities (guṇas) are isolated. (110)
Indeed, the means for the attainment of liberation is that which is called discriminative discernment (vivekakhyāti).
That discernment, being entirely free from false knowledge, is the cause of liberation. (111)

The "object of sight" (*dṛśya*) consists of the elements and the sense organs; the "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) is consciousness (*caitanya*). Due to the proximity of the object of sight, the *puruṣa* appears as if it were subject to transformation; due to the proximity of the *puruṣa*, the object of sight appears as if it were conscious. This proximity—or indeed conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—is the cause of what is to be abandoned (*heya*). Just as well-adorned objects exist for the sake of enjoyment by someone, so too does the object of sight proceed for the sake of being seen by the *puruṣa*. Ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases for the liberated one, but not for all. The absence of this conjunction, which has ignorance as its cause, is liberation (*hāna*). The path to attaining that is discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*).
The pure wisdom of the yogi arises in seven ways;
having attained this sevenfold wisdom, the yogi enjoys absolute liberation.

1. "All that is to be known has been known; there is nothing whatsoever remaining to be known"—this is the first [verse]. 2. "All that is to be abandoned has been abandoned; there is nothing whatsoever remaining to be abandoned"—this is the second. 3. "All that is to be attained has been attained; there is nothing whatsoever for me to attain"—this is the third.
4. "All that was to be done has been done; there is nothing further for me to do"—this is the fourth [state].
5. "The principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva) has accomplished its purpose"—this is the fifth.
6. "The qualities (guṇas) have fulfilled their office"—this is the sixth.
7. "I am beyond qualities (guṇātīta), established in my own essential nature alone, the single flavor of Being-Consciousness"—this is the seventh [state].
For the yogi, the perfection of the goal is dependent upon practice;
the performance of the limbs of yoga is the means for the restraint of the mind. (113)
Through the practice of the limbs of yoga, impurity is certainly destroyed;
and upon the destruction of impurity, great discernment truly shines forth. (114)

The restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), as well as the posture (āsana) performed with faith, along with breath control (prāṇāyāma) in its true essence and likewise withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra). || 115 ||
Retention, meditation, and yoga—these various limbs of yoga—are not limited by anything; they are universal and constitute the Great Vow.
Non-violence toward all beings through the actions of mind, speech, and body—this must be practiced everywhere and at all times by those seeking liberation. 117.
In that same manner, each subsequent group of seven [limbs] should be understood as dependent upon the preceding one;
therefore, for one desiring liberation, the practice of these limbs of yoga is primary.
When the outward-flowing power is restrained by the limbs of yoga, then the truth increases, as do physical and mental strength. || 119 ||
1. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness—these are the *yamas*.
2. Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord—these are the *niyamas*.
3. The lotus, the swastika, and others—these are the *āsanas*.
4. Prāṇāyāma is the cessation of the flow of inhalation and exhalation.
5. Pratyāhāra is the withdrawal of the senses so that they conform to the nature of the mind.
6. Dhāraṇā is the fixing of the mind on various specific locations.
7. Meditation (dhyāna) is the continuous flow of a single form;
8. Samādhi is the manifestation of the object of meditation in its entirety, without doubt.
Furthermore, the restraints (yamas), when not limited by species, place, time, or circumstance, are called great vows (mahāvratas).
Through their correct practice, the various powers are perfected. When non-violence is firmly established, one abides in a state free from enmity. (120)
For when one is firmly established in truth alone, that speech arises free from clouds;
and through non-stealing alone, the acquisition of jewels is accomplished.
By being firmly established in celibacy, the yogi attains mastery;
when all grasping is abandoned, he knows the true nature of birth.
From purity comes cleanliness of one's own body, as well as a sense of revulsion [toward impurity] and non-association with others;
from contentment comes the attainment of happiness, for which there is no comparison whatsoever. (123)
Austerity properly undertaken with faith destroys impurity;
therefore, the yogi effortlessly attains mastery over the body and the senses.
Through the study of the scriptures and other means, the direct vision of one's chosen deities is accomplished;
for divine deities and sages abide within the practice of yoga. (125)
One should properly adopt that seat which is stable and provides comfort;
for when the mind ceases its effort, concentration of the mind becomes firm. (126)
One who knows the posture is not overcome by dualities such as cold and heat;
having first conquered those, one should strive for the restraint of the vital air.
The grasping of the external air through the nose is called *pūraka* (inhalation);
thereafter, its proper expulsion is designated as *recaka* (exhalation). 128.
The cessation of the movement of those two [breaths] is proclaimed as prāṇāyāma;
it is said to be threefold: inhalation (pūraka), exhalation (recaka), and retention (kumbhaka). || 129 ||
The fourth state is considered to be the Kevala (the absolute), which is long, subtle, and well-known;
for in the Kevala, the vital breath exists devoid of inhalation and exhalation.
Through breath control (prāṇāyāma), the veil over the light is certainly destroyed;
then the mind becomes pure and fit for concentration (dhāraṇā). 131.
Dhāraṇā is the binding of the mind in locations such as the navel-cakra;
dhyāna is the continuous flow of mental modifications; and samādhi is that same flow when it is uninterrupted. (132)
Meditation, which is designated as "samādhi," manifests in the form of the object of meditation;
yet, within that samādhi consisting of mental conditions, form is not empty in reality.
The technical term for the bonds, meditations, and concentrations is *saṃyama* in Yoga;
through the perfection of *saṃyama* alone, the lamp of wisdom shines forth. (134)
Likewise, by conquering each individual stage, the mind's transition to the next is surely accomplished; thereby, wisdom is set ablaze. (135)
These three are considered the internal limbs (antaraṅga) because they follow the accomplishment of concentration (samādhi);
even for seedless yoga (nirbīja-yoga), these three are remembered as the external limbs (bahiraṅga).

In the *Yogasandarbha*, "saṃyama" is defined as the triad of *dhāraṇā* (concentration), *dhyāna* (meditation), and *samādhi* (absorption). When the mind, free from other cognitions, becomes a continuous flow of similar cognitions regarding a single object, manifesting only that true reality, it should be known as *saṃyama*. Such a power of the mind, in the form of one-pointedness, must be accomplished. Among the eight limbs, *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* are internal (*antaraṅga*) compared to the five beginning with *yama*; these three directly assist the essential nature [of the self].
However, because they are not direct causes for seedless (*nirbīja*) *samādhi*, they are considered external (*bahiraṅga*) to that.
The transformation of the mind, which is unstable by nature, is said to be threefold:
cessation (nirodha), meditative absorption (samādhi), and that which is called one-pointedness (ekāgratā). || 137 ||
The complete overcoming of emergence and the arising of cessation, as well as the manifold course of the formative forces (saṃskāra), is called "cessation" (nirodha). || 138 ||
The transformation of meditative concentration (samādhi) consists of two mental qualities:
the attainment of all objects without exhaustion, as well as the arising of perfect one-pointedness. || 139 ||

Furthermore, when the subsided and the arisen states are identical in their causal conditions, the transformation of the nature of the mind takes the form of one-pointedness regarding the object of knowledge. (140)

The three stages known as the distracted (*kṣipta*), the dull (*mūḍha*), and the scattered (*vikṣipta*) constitute the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*). Among these, the *kṣipta* is unstable due to the predominance of the quality of passion (*rajas*); the *mūḍha* is characterized by the predominance of the quality of darkness (*tamas*); and the *vikṣipta* is that mind which, due to the predominance of goodness (*sattva*), avoids the means of suffering and engages exclusively with the means of pleasure, such as sound and so forth, yet remains distinguished by passion. The "overpowering of the impressions of emergence" refers to the burning away of these three states beginning with the distracted. The "arising of the impressions of restraint" refers to the firm establishment [of the mind] on the path that is manifest.

The transformation occurring at the time of cessation makes the mind steady; this is the transformation of cessation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*). The waning of the mind’s capacity for all objects and the arising of one-pointedness is the transformation of concentration (*samādhi-pariṇāma*). In that state, two similar cognitions—one past and one presently arising—constitute the "transformation of one-pointedness" (*ekāgratā-pariṇāma*). When each preceding cognition of the same kind perishes, another cognition of the same kind arises. These very properties (*dharma*) have been explained in relation to the elements (*bhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*): it is the relinquishing of one property and the acquisition of another property.
The first transformation would belong to the substrate (dharmin) which possesses a gross form. || 141 ||

Furthermore, the differentiation of phenomena according to the distinctions of time, such as the past and so forth, is indeed the second transformation called "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) in reality. (142)
In the case of a cow and so forth, there are childhood, youth, adolescence, and likewise old age;
these constitute the three states, and the final one is transformation (pariṇāma). (143)

The transformation of attributes (*dharmapariṇāma*) is the acquisition of another attribute by a single substrate (*dharmin*) upon the cessation of its previous attribute; for example, the state of being a jar resulting from clay’s relinquishing of its state as a lump. The transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*) consists in the attainment of a past state by the present state, producing differentiation through the distinction of time. The transformation of condition (*avasthāpariṇāma*) takes the form of distinctions such as antiquity and modernity. Indeed, there are three types of attributes belonging to a substrate: the attribute itself, the capacity (*yogyatā*) within the substrates, and the activity residing in the attribute.
This threefold nature of the attribute dependent on its operation is the view of the author of the Sūtras. (144)
Past, present, and likewise future phenomena—within all of them, that which possesses the qualities (dharma) always exists as distinct from them. (145)
Whatever sequence brings about the immediate succession of a given phenomenon, that sequence is the constant cause of diversity in its transformation. (146)
Through *saṃyama* upon the three transformations, the yogi becomes possessed of knowledge regarding all things, whether past or future. (147)
For the confusion of word, object, and cognition is rooted in superimposition.
Through *saṃyama* upon their distinction, there arises knowledge of the cries of all living beings. (148)

Formations are said to be of two kinds: latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and dispositions (*āśaya*). Latent impressions are the cause of memory, while dispositions are the cause of maturation (*vipāka*). (149)
Indeed, through the direct realization of these formative predispositions (saṃskāras) in their true nature, knowledge of one's own and others' previous births arises. || 150 ||
Through *saṃyama* upon the mental modification (*pratyaya*), knowledge of another's mind arises;
however, that [knowledge] is said not to include its object, because it is inseparable from one's own mind. (151)
The yogin suppresses that power of being perceived through *saṃyama*;
consequently, the disappearance of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) occurs within it. || 152 ||
The wise declare that the karma which results in lifespan is also twofold:
the first is "with onset" (sopakrama), and the second is "without onset" (nirupakrama). || 153 ||
Karma that yields its fruit with intense velocity is called "with effort" (sopakrama); that which proceeds with slow velocity is said to be "without effort" (nirupakrama). // 154 //
But by restraining these two, the yogi attains great knowledge;
likewise, through the omens (ariṣṭas), he knows the approaching arrival of death. || 155 ||

Through the practice of concentration on mental cultivation and restraint, the yogi likewise attains that specific supreme and swift power by means of restraint directed toward elephants and other such beings. || 156 ||
Through the luminous activity [of the mind] and by means of the projection of light, cognition arises regarding that which is subtle, remote, or obstructed. (157)
Through restraint upon the sun, knowledge of the entire world arises;
and through restraint upon the moon and the pole star (dhruva), there is knowledge of the arrangement of the stars and so forth.
Through *saṃyama* on the navel-center (*nābhicakra*), there arises the awakening of poetry;
and through *saṃyama* on the hollow of the throat (*kaṇṭhakūpa*), there is the destruction of hunger and thirst. (159)
Through restraint, the practitioner remains steady while focused on the *kūrmanāḍī*;
likewise, having directed [the mind] to the *suṣumnā*, he indeed beholds the perfected ones (*siddhas*).
Having practiced *saṃyama* on the intuitive faculty (*pratibhā*), one knows everything with ease;
likewise, having fixed the mind on the heart, the practitioner of *saṃyama* knows [the thoughts]. (161)
The primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) are always absolutely unmixed;
yet experience consists in being devoid of that distinction, and in reality, it exists because [the self] has another as its purpose. || 162 ||
Having thoroughly understood that [Self] for the sake of others, and having practiced self-restraint in his own chariot, the yogi knows that Puruṣa, the knower, with ease. (163)
Through *saṃyama* upon the Puruṣa, the yogi attains many perfections (*siddhis*), namely:
intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*), auditory knowledge (*śrāvaṇa*), and likewise that which is called tactile knowledge (*vedanā*). (164)

The various kinds of supernatural powers (siddhis), such as the mirror-like [clairvoyance], the power of taste, and the power of hearing, are called siddhis because they cause the senses to perceive divine objects. 165.

Furthermore, those perfections such as intuitive insight (*prātibha*) are obstacles to yoga; they are indeed perfections belonging to the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*). Therefore, they should be abandoned by those seeking liberation.
Through the destruction of the bonds of karma, the yogi, by perceiving the movement of the mind,
then effortlessly casts that very mind into other bodies.
Whether in rising mud, water, or among thorns and the like, the yogi attains the power of upward movement (utkrānti) through the power of the udāna and vyāna breaths. || 168 ||
The one who possesses the yoga of the *samāna* breath blazes like fire;
space (*ākāśa*) is the foundation of all sounds, an ocean of sound. (169)
By practicing saṃyama on the connection between the ākāśa-tattva and the ears,
the yogi attains divine hearing, which is the cause of all sound.

Just as one flies through the sky by means of the meditative attainment of lightness like cotton, so too does the yogi fly once he has performed *saṃyama* upon the connection between the body and space. 171.
Through saṃyama upon the gross form, the subtle essence, as well as the inherence and the purposefulness of the five elements, the practitioner of saṃyama attains mastery over them. (172)
By that very [means], the attainment of the supernatural powers (siddhis), beginning with atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, is accomplished;
as well as the perfection of the body, its completion, and the state of being unconquerable by others through one's qualities (dharmas). 173.
Apprehension, essential nature, and likewise the connection with the sense of "I"—by practicing *saṃyama* upon these, the practitioner of *saṃyama* conquers the senses. (174)

Having correctly understood the distinction between the intellect and the person, the practitioner of self-restraint indeed becomes omniscient and the sovereign controller of all states of being. || 176 ||
Through that dispassion, by the destruction of the seeds of all defects, the seer attains isolation—the stable abiding in one's own true nature. || 177 ||
Even when invited by the gods to taste the flavors of various enjoyments,
the yogi should not give way to attachment or pride, for he has transcended all that is undesirable.
Through *saṃyama* upon the moment and its sequence, the yogi soon attains the liberating knowledge, perfected by discernment, which results from the total destruction of all [impurities]. (179)

For when there is equality in purity between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), isolation (kaivalya) occurs; this results from the completion of the predominance of the quality of goodness (sattva) and from the seer’s perception of his own true nature. 180.
Indeed, these five kinds of accomplishments (siddhis) are achieved through birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative absorption (samādhi). || 181 ||
The state of having a body distinct from those of humans and others is to be understood as resulting from the influx of *prakṛti*, caused by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). (182)
Dharma and the other [factors] are never the actual instigators of those signs; rather, the effect arises through a distinction in the substratum, as the field-owner is the illustration here. (183)
When the yogi creates another body by his own power,
then the creative minds therein arise solely from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
For when there is a multiplicity of activities, a single mind is the instigator;
even in that case, the mind born of meditative concentration is devoid of the latent impressions of karma.
In general, however, the foot of karma is complete;
it is white for those of virtuous soul alone, while it is black for those of evil soul. (186)
For others, that [result] may be white or black, but for yogins it is never so;
and the maturation (vipāka) will correspond in nature to each respective type of karma.
The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that correspond to those [actions] become manifest through their maturation;
thus, among gods, animals, and humans, the experience is indeed the same. (188)

Since the identity of memory and mental impression (saṃskāra) is established in their nature, therefore [the object], though separated by signs such as genus and so forth, remains immediate. || 189 ||

Just as a farmer, desiring to lead water from one field to another, performs only the removal of obstructions and barriers, so too dharma and the other causes are merely the instigators of the transformation of the *prakṛtis*. Among the various activities of the minds produced from the ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*) of a yogin, the mind of the yogin alone is the single instigator. Among the five types of minds beginning with those born of birth, it is specifically the mind born of meditation that is free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Among the fourfold classification of karma—namely, white (*śukla*), black (*kṛṣṇa*), white-and-black (*śukla-kṛṣṇa*), and neither-white-nor-black (*aśukla-akṛṣṇa*)—it is the fourth type of yoga for which there is a fruit corresponding exactly to its nature. Furthermore, among all beings, there is the manifestation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that correspond to those fruits. From these impressions comes memory, from memory comes experience (*bhoga*), and from the experience of yoga, there arise again impressions, memory, and so forth. Therefore, the sense is this: even those impressions separated by hundreds of births, vast distances, or hundreds of cosmic cycles (*kalpa*) remain capable of producing their effects as if they were not separated at all.

The beginninglessness of latent impressions (vāsanās) is likewise due to the eternity of the desire for existence; the mind, pierced by those impressions, is capable of providing experience for consciousness (citi). 190.
The latent predispositions (vāsanās) are indeed comprised of causes, fruits, bases, and objects;
however, in the absence of these causes and so forth, they undergo total destruction in every respect. (191)

Latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are not only devoid of manifestation, but are also beginningless. These latent impressions proceed by taking causes and so forth as their objects. In this regard, the cause is either direct or indirect—namely, ignorance (*avidyā*); the fruit is the body and so forth, as well as memory and so forth; the substratum is the mind (*citta*); and the object of support (*ālambana*) should be understood as being exactly the same for the latent impressions as it is for experience. In the absence of these, there is also the absence of latent impressions. How could latent impressions cease if the nature of substance (*dravyatva*) were possible?
Thus, a person might at some point doubt the destruction of latent impressions. (192)
Past and future phenomena, as well as the mind, are by their very nature the substratum (dharmin).
This is the distinction among phenomena alone; it is devoid of any distinction within the substratum itself. (193)
Indeed, these phenomena belonging to the three times are, in reality, both manifest and subtle;
because they are situated within the *guṇas*, they consist of the nature of the *guṇas*. (194)

Manifested phenomena are those existing in the present; subtle phenomena, which have the elements and so forth as their objects, are those that exist in the past and future within the elements and the sense organs. (195)
The reality of the qualities (guṇas) is held to be one by virtue of their relationship as constituent parts and the whole;
for the transformation of many things, such as oil and so forth, is like that of a lamp. || 196 ||

Among the three qualities (guṇas), in some instances sattva is predominant, in some rajas, and in others tamas; thus there exists a relationship of primary and secondary among the qualities. Although there are three qualities, nevertheless, because they stand in the relation of primary and secondary, the object remains a single entity. Just as oil, wick, and fire constitute a single transformation known as a lamp, so too is this [the case with the qualities].
Various kinds of knowledge are observed even regarding a single type of object; therefore, it is certain that the paths of knowledge and the object are distinct. (197)

In a single woman endowed with beauty and grace, there is pleasure for the man of passion, hatred for the co-wife, indifference for the Vedāntin, and revulsion for the wandering mendicant; thus, a diversity of cognitions is observed toward a single object.
Therefore, cognition is distinct from its object. Consequently, there is no proof for the destruction of the mind, and thus the mind possesses independence.
And in this way, the Sūtra rejects an object that co-exists with cognition. (198)

"Let it be granted that the object is distinct from cognition; nevertheless, since it is manifested by cognition alone and is an object of enjoyment like pleasure and so forth, the view that the object is co-existent with cognition is correct," he says. The object is independent and common to all people, whereas the minds functioning for each individual person are independent [of one another].
Like iron, the mind is colored by the object;
it takes up that [object] and abandons another, for it is thus characterized as known and unknown. (199)
The mental modification is always known by the Puruṣa who dwells within it as its witness;
for since the mind undergoes transformation, the Puruṣa remains entirely free from that change.
This mind never possesses its own appearance, because it is an object of perception, like fire;
for fire, when concealed by darkness, does not shine forth beforehand. (201)

If it is argued that, like fire, the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) themselves might be self-luminous, rendering superfluous a Puruṣa who perceives those modifications—the answer is no. This is because the mind (*citta*), being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*) like the color blue and so forth, cannot be self-illuminating; rather, it requires a seer distinct from itself. The point is that since the mind possesses attributes such as luminosity and non-luminosity, even the analogy of fire and the like is inapplicable here due to the causal disparity between the *guṇas*.
The mind does not grasp both its own nature and an object simultaneously;
therefore, it appears as its own reflection, and thus it is not regarded as a mere object.
If [the object] were apprehended through another mental modification (*vṛtti*), there would be an over-extension regarding that modification;
for if there were a cognition of infinite modifications, there would be a confusion of infinite memories. (203)
That consciousness is unmixed, consisting in the perception of its own mental modification; yet, when the nature of the mental modification arises, it likewise takes on that form. (204)
That mental consciousness, colored by the object to be thought about, has existence as its object; for the mind, colored by both the seer and the seen, is said to have itself as its object. (205)
Because it functions through aggregation, the mind is said to exist for the sake of another;
though variegated by incalculable formative forces (saṃskāra), it is like a house.
He who, being self-restrained, knows the distinction between the sevenfold sheaths and the Person— for him,
the mental preoccupation with the nature of the self then ceases.
Due to ignorance, the mind is filled with sense objects; however, upon the arising of knowledge, it turns toward liberation through the power of discriminative discernment, O Bhārata.
Those mental factors that arise during the intervals between concentrations should be understood as being destroyed by the impressions of emergence, due to the dissolution of the mind. (209)
Just as afflictions do not sprout when their seeds have been burnt by fire, so too are former formative predispositions destroyed, being consumed by knowledge. (210)
For one who is free from passion even regarding discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), there arises the "cloud of dharma" (*dharmamegha*) samādhi;
this samādhi, arising from the clear manifestation of discrimination (*vivekakhyāti*), should be known as the destroyer of the afflictions (*kleśa*). (211)
The culmination of clear comprehension is indeed the rain-cloud of Dharma;
it is the great path of Yoga that bestows absolute liberation. || 212 ||
Through the attainment of that [knowledge], all afflictions such as ignorance and the rest are destroyed; and the entire store of latent impressions of karma becomes completely annihilated. (213)
Completely liberated from all afflictions and devoid of all defects, infinite knowledge arises; for the object of knowledge appears as something slight.
But when the gunas have achieved their purpose, through the arising of samādhi, the sequence of transformation conducive to experience comes to an end. (215)

The state of being subject to transformation (pariṇāminityatā) belongs to the qualities (guṇas) as they exist in the present; the state of being eternally immutable (kūṭasthanityatā) belongs to the Person (puruṣa). That [state] is to be understood as the permanence common to both. || 216 ||
The sequence of the object of knowledge consists of pairs of moments and is based on a succession of moments;
in reality, the sequence of transformation is to be grasped through its final limit. (217)

With the arising of samādhi, the sequence of transformation of the qualities (guṇas), which had served their purpose and were engaged in providing experience, comes to an end. A moment (kṣaṇa) is the indicator of that sequence; the sequence itself consists of a collection of such moments and is to be grasped by extracting it from the "other end" (aparānta). As stated in the *Yogasudhākara*: "In the case of clay, the 'prior end' is the lump and the 'other end' is the particle.
When the purpose of the Puruṣa has been accomplished, the guṇa, now devoid of that [purpose] and delusive, enters into dissolution (pratiprasava) and remains forever in its isolated state. (218)
Then, liberated from bondage, the person is forever devoid of qualities;
established in its own nature through yoga, it then becomes what is called consciousness. || 219 ||
Bondage and liberation never belong to the body, nor indeed to the person (puruṣa). This bondage is the passion of the mind; non-liberation is the state of being devoid of dispassion.
Having relied upon the great Pātañjala Sūtra, as well as the commentary by Vyāsa,
and the words of Vācaspati and others, according to their true meaning.
This commentary on the Yoga Sūtras has been composed by me in verse;
I am merely the instrument here, while the cause is the grace of my Guru.
